name: AM (Amplitude Modulation)
explainer: Signal strength (amplitude) varies to carry sound. Simple and tolerant of weak-signal fading, and lets a stronger station be heard over a weaker one on the same frequency instead of blocking it outright.
when_used: AM/mediumwave broadcast, shortwave broadcast, airband voice.

name: FM / NFM (Narrowband Frequency Modulation)
explainer: Signal frequency varies slightly to carry sound. Used for most two-way land-mobile voice. Generally clearer than AM in strong-signal conditions, but the weaker of two same-frequency signals is usually blocked entirely (the 'capture effect') rather than heard faintly underneath.
when_used: Ham repeaters/simplex, GMRS/FRS/MURS, marine VHF, NOAA Weather Radio, railroad, most public-safety.

name: WFM (Wideband FM)
explainer: Wide-deviation FM used for commercial FM broadcast - much higher audio fidelity than narrowband FM, but uses far more bandwidth. On a wideband receiver, WFM is usually a separate mode setting from (N)FM, not the same one.

name: USB (Upper Sideband)
explainer: A form of single-sideband voice (roughly half of an AM signal, more efficient for a given power). Used by amateur-radio convention above 10 MHz, plus HF airband and marine SSB. Sounds badly garbled if tuned even slightly off-frequency - fine adjustment matters.
when_used: Amateur bands 30m and up (by convention), HF airband voice, marine SSB.

name: LSB (Lower Sideband)
explainer: The other half of single-sideband voice - same technical concept as USB, just the other sideband. Used by amateur-radio convention on 160m/80m/60m/40m. The USB/LSB split by band is a long-standing operating custom, not a technical requirement.

name: CW (Continuous Wave / Morse Code)
explainer: The carrier is simply switched on and off to send Morse code - no voice. Extremely narrow bandwidth, so CW signals can often be copied through noise/interference where a voice signal couldn't.
when_used: Common at the edges of amateur HF bands.
